A can of soda is taken out of a refrigerator and left in a room that stays at a constant temperature of $32{\,}^{∘}\text{C}.$ The soda’s temperature $T(t)$ (in degrees Celsius) can be modeled by the differential equation:

$$
\frac{dT}{dt}=k(32-T),
$$

where $t\ge 0$ is the time, measured in minutes, and $k>0$ is a constant. The initial temperature of the soda is $5{\,}^{∘}\text{C},$ and after $10$ minutes, the soda has warmed to $27{\,}^{∘}\text{C}.$ To the nearest minute, how long does it take for the soda to reach $29{\,}^{∘}\text{C}?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We're told that the temperature of the can is modeled by the inhibited growth equation

$$
\frac{dT}{dt}=k(32-T).
$$

We separate variables and integrate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dT}{32-T} & =k\,dt \\ \int \frac{dT}{32-T} & =\int k\,dt \\ -\operatorname{ln}⁡|32-T| & =kt+C\end{aligned}
$$

Since this is the solution to an inhibited growth equation, we have $32-T>0$ for all $t\ge 0.$ Next, we solve for $T(t),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}32-T & ={e}^{-kt-C} \\ 32-T & ={e}^{-C}{e}^{-kt} \\ 32-T & =K{e}^{-kt} \\ T & =32-K{e}^{-kt}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $K={e}^{-C}$ is a constant of integration.

We're told that the initial temperature was $5{\,}^{∘}\text{C}.$ So, we apply the initial condition $T(0)=5,$ and solve for $K:$

$$
\begin{aligned}5 & =32-K{e}^{0} \\ 5 & =32-K \\ K & =27\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to our initial value problem is

$$
T(t)=32-27{e}^{-kt}.
$$

We're also told that, after $10$ minutes, the temperature of the soda was $27{\,}^{∘}\text{C}.$ So, applying the condition $T(10)=27,$  we can solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}27 & =32-27{e}^{-10k} \\ 5 & =27{e}^{-10k} \\ {e}^{-10k} & =\frac{5}{27} \\ -10k & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{5}{27}) \\ k & =-\frac{1}{10}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{5}{27})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, let ${t}_{1}$  be the time when the soda can reaches $29{\,}^{∘}\text{C}.$ Then, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}T({t}_{1}) & =29 \\ 32-27{e}^{-k{t}_{1}} & =29 \\ 3 & =27{e}^{-k{t}_{1}} \\ {e}^{-k{t}_{1}} & =\frac{1}{9} \\ -k{t}_{1} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{9}) \\ {t}_{1} & =-\frac{1}{k}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{9})\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the value of $k,$ we get:

$$
{t}_{1}=\frac{-\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{9})}{-\frac{1}{10}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{5}{27})}=13.029…≈13\text{ }\text{minutes},
$$

rounded to the nearest minute.

Since this is the solution to an inhibited growth equation, we have $1200-P>0$ for all $t\ge 0.$ Next, we solve for $P(t),$ as follows:

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}P(12) & =1119 \\ 1200-K{e}^{-12k} & =1119 \\ K{e}^{-12k} & =81.\end{aligned}

question.:question/problem:
A small bakery produces loaves of bread. The owner knows that the bakery can produce a maximum of $800$ loaves a day; however, current production is below this maximum. Since she started monitoring, the bakers produced $700$ loaves and $740$ loaves on days $5$ and $10,$ respectively. How many loaves do they produce on day $45?$ Round your answer to the nearest integer.

*Hint: You may assume that the bread production $E(t)$ increases at a rate that obeys an inhibited growth model, where $t$ is the time, in days.*
question.:question/worked-solution:
The rate at which the bread production $E(t)$ changes is proportional to the difference between the maximum possible bread production and its current bread production. Therefore, we have the inhibited growth equation

$$
\frac{dE}{dt}=k(a-E),
$$

where $a$ is the maximum production of the bakery, and $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality.

In our case, $a=800$ loaves, and we have

$$
\frac{dE}{dt}=k(800-E).
$$

First, we integrate our differential equation by separating the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dE}{800-E} & =k\,dt \\ \int \frac{dE}{800-E} & =\int k\,\text{d}t \\ -\operatorname{ln}⁡|800-E| & =kt+C\end{aligned}
$$

Since this is the solution to an inhibited growth equation, we have $800-E>0$ for all $t\ge 0.$ Next, we solve for $E(t),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}800-E & ={e}^{-kt-C} \\ 800-E & ={e}^{-C}{e}^{-kt} \\ 800-E & =K{e}^{-kt} \\ E & =800-K{e}^{-kt}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $K={e}^{-C}$ is a constant of integration.

We're told that, on day $5,$ the bread production was $700$ loaves. So, applying the condition $E(5)=700,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}E(5) & =700 \\ 800-K{e}^{-5k} & =700 \\ K{e}^{-5k} & =100.\end{aligned}
$$

We're also told that, on day $10,$ the bread production was $740$ loaves. So, applying the condition $E(10)=740,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}E(10) & =740 \\ 800-K{e}^{-10k} & =740 \\ K{e}^{-10k} & =60.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, by dividing the result of the first condition by the result of the second, we can solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{K{e}^{-5k}}{K{e}^{-10k}} & =\frac{100}{60} \\ {e}^{5k} & =\frac{5}{3} \\ 5k & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{5}{3}) \\ k & =\frac{1}{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{5}{3})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting back into the result of the first condition, we solve for $K:$

$$
\begin{aligned}K{e}^{-5\cdot (1/5)\operatorname{ln}⁡(5/3)} & =100 \\ K & =100{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5/3)} \\ K & =\frac{500}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following expression for $E(t):$

$$
E(t)=800-\frac{500}{3}{e}^{-(t/5)\operatorname{ln}⁡(5/3)}
$$

Finally, the number of loaves baked on day $t=45$ is

$$
E(45)=800-\frac{500}{3}{e}^{-(45/5)\operatorname{ln}⁡(5/3)}≈798.320…≈798\,\text{loaves},
$$

rounded to the nearest integer.
